## Executive Summary {.unnumbered}

> **Recommendation.** Exporters of AI-enabled products to multiple markets
> should adopt the EU AI Act risk-classification as their internal baseline by
> Q3 2026. It is the most prescriptive regime, so building to it first reduces
> rework when conforming to the lighter US (NIST RMF) and UK frameworks. Firms
> selling only domestically in Korea should prioritize KR AI Act tier-2
> documentation instead.

The five regimes surveyed below differ sharply on whether compliance is
mandatory, how heavy the penalties are, and how long a conformity assessment
takes. The chart in the [Data](#data) section quantifies that last dimension —
the *lead time* a vendor needs before a product can ship — which is often the
binding constraint in practice, not the headline penalty.

## Background

"AI regulation" is not one thing. By mid-2026 the landscape splits into two
philosophies:

- **Prescriptive, mandatory regimes** that classify systems into risk tiers and
  attach hard penalties — the EU AI Act, Korea's AI Act, and Canada's proposed
  AIDA.
- **Principles-based, voluntary frameworks** that offer a structured process
  but no statutory penalty — the US NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the
  UK's "pro-innovation" approach.

A vendor selling across these markets cannot pick one. The practical question
is which framework to build to *first* so the others come cheaply.

## Data {#data}

The comparison matrix lives in `data/regulation_matrix.csv`. The chunk below
loads it with pandas, renders it as a table, and plots the conformity lead time
each regime demands.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-matrix
#| tbl-cap: "Regulatory comparison matrix (source: data/regulation_matrix.csv)"
import pandas as pd

reg = pd.read_csv("data/regulation_matrix.csv")
reg
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-leadtime
#| fig-cap: "Conformity lead time before a product can ship (months)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ordered = reg.sort_values("conformity_lead_months", ascending=True)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.2))
plt.barh(ordered["jurisdiction"], ordered["conformity_lead_months"])
plt.xlabel("Lead time to conformity (months)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The voluntary regimes (UK, NIST) clear in 2–3 months; the EU AI Act's
high-risk conformity path is the longest at nine months. That gap, not the fine
schedule, is what determines launch dates.

## Findings

1. **Mandatory ≠ slow, but prescriptive does.** The EU and Canada regimes carry
   both the largest penalties and the longest lead times. Korea is mandatory yet
   noticeably faster to clear.
2. **Voluntary frameworks are becoming de-facto mandatory.** NIST RMF has no
   statutory penalty, but it is increasingly written into US federal and
   enterprise procurement contracts, so ignoring it costs deals rather than fines.
3. **The EU is the binding baseline.** Because it is the strictest on every
   axis, a product built to EU high-risk standards largely satisfies the others
   with documentation mapping rather than re-engineering.

## Recommendations

| If your product is... | Then prioritize |
|------------------------|-----------------|
| EU-bound, high-risk    | EU AI Act conformity assessment — start ≥ 9 months out |
| US federal-bound       | NIST RMF mapping + contract clauses |
| KR domestic only       | KR AI Act tier-2 documentation |
| Multi-jurisdiction     | EU AI Act baseline, then map to the rest |
| Early-stage / UK pilot | UK pro-innovation self-assessment, revisit at scale |

## Methodology

Penalty figures are normalized to USD millions for comparability and are
indicative ceilings, not expected fines. Lead-time estimates synthesize
published conformity-assessment guidance and practitioner interviews; they
describe a mid-sized vendor (~$10M ARR) without prior compliance tooling. The
underlying values are editable in `data/regulation_matrix.csv` — re-render to
update every table and chart.
